In this passage, gratitude is not merely a feeling that follows the blessing — it is bound up with the very sign that the blessing has come.

Ibn Kathir closes his commentary here by noting that he will elaborate more on this subject at the beginning of Surah Maryam (chapter 19), Allah willing.

passages.title: The angels' address to Mary's chosen purity
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is

These three ayat record a moment when angels address Maryam directly. They tell her what Allah has done for her — chosen her, purified her, chosen her above the women of the nations — and then, in the very next ayah, tell her what she must do: be devout to her Lord, prostrate, and bow with those who bow. The passage then turns from Maryam toward the Prophet ﷺ himself (ayah 44): *you were not there.* You were not present when the pens were cast; you were not present when they disputed. This is news of the unseen, revealed to you.

So the unit holds together as a single arc: **honour granted (42) → honour answered with worship (43) → and the whole account offered as proof that the one reciting it is a Prophet (44).**

---

## Ayah 42: chosen, purified, chosen again

Ibn Kathir notes that the angels spoke to Maryam **by Allah's command** — this was not their own initiative but a message delivered on His behalf. And he lists precisely why she was chosen: **her service to Him, her modesty, her honour, her innocence, and her conviction**, and because of her virtue over the women of the world.

Notice that this is a description of a life, not of a lucky accident. Allah's choosing is real and free — He chooses whom He wills — and Ibn Kathir ties it here to what she actually was: a servant, modest, honourable, innocent, certain in faith.

The wording of the ayah also names the choosing twice. Allah **chose** her — and **chose her above the women of the nations**; Ibn Kathir glosses this second phrase as her virtue over the women of the world. And between the two, the ayah places **purification**.

---

## "Above the women of the nations" — how far does it reach?

This phrase has been discussed carefully, because other reports also praise other women, and a reader may wonder how they fit together. The two sources in front of us each take up the question in their own way.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** speaks to it directly: the words *"and has chosen you over women of all the worlds"* in ayah 42 refer to **all women in that period of time**. Therefore, Maʿārif says, the statement appearing in hadith that **Fatimah is the foremost among the women of Paradise** does not contradict this ayah. (The source conveys this teaching without naming a collection for it, so it is passed on here as the meaning conveyed, not attributed to any particular book.)

**Ibn Kathir** treats the ayah under a heading of his own: *"The Virtue of Maryam Over the Women of Her Time."* Under it he brings these narrations:

**At-Tirmidhi** recorded that ʿAli bin Abi Talib said: *"I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say:* **'The best woman (in her time) was Maryam, daughter of ʿImran, and the best woman (of the Prophet's time) is Khadijah (his wife), daughter of Khuwaylid.'"** Ibn Kathir adds that **the Two Sahihs** recorded this hadith.

Read the wording closely and you see each woman paired with a time: Maryam, the best woman in her time; Khadijah, the best woman of the Prophet's time.

**Ibn Jarir** recorded that Abu Musa al-Ashʿari said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"Many men achieved perfection, but among women, only Maryam the daughter of ʿImran and Asiah, the wife of Firʿawn, achieved perfection."** Ibn Kathir notes that **the Six, with the exception of Abu Dawud**, recorded it, and that **al-Bukhari's** wording reads: *"Many men reached the level of perfection, but no woman reached such a level except Asiah, the wife of Firʿawn, and Maryam, the daughter of ʿImran. The superiority of ʿA'ishah (his wife) to other women is like the superiority of Tharid* (a meat and bread dish) *to other meals."* Ibn Kathir mentions that he gathered the various chains of narration and wordings of this hadith in the story of ʿIsa, son of Maryam, in his book *Al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah*.

Two names stand together in that narration: Maryam, and Asiah the wife of Firʿawn. Whatever else separated their lives, the hadith places them side by side among those who reached perfection.

---

## Ayah 43: the honour turns instantly into a command

The angels do not leave Maryam with a compliment. In ayah 43 they say: **"O Maryam! Be devout to your Lord, prostrate yourself, and bow down with those who bow."**

Ibn Kathir explains that the angels **commanded Maryam to increase acts of worship** — humbleness, submission, prostration, bowing, and so forth — *"so that she would acquire what Allah had decreed for her, as a test for her."* And he adds that this test **also earned her a higher grade in this life and the Hereafter**, for through it Allah demonstrated His might by creating a son inside her without male intervention.

This is the hinge of the passage. Being chosen is not a resting place; it is a summons to more worship, and that worship is what readies her for what Allah had decreed. In Ibn Kathir's reading the test and the elevation are the same event seen from two sides.

**The word *qunut*.** The command *iqnutī* comes from *qunūt*. Ibn Kathir defines it plainly: **it means to submit with humbleness**. It is not merely carrying out an order; it is submission with lowliness before the One obeyed. He points to Allah's words elsewhere to fix the sense: *"Nay, to Him belongs all that is in the heavens and on earth, and all surrender with obedience (**Qanitun**) to Him"* (al-Baqarah 2:116).

Note also the order the ayah gives: **be devout → prostrate → bow.**

**"With those who bow" — a lesson in how we bow.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to something easy to read past. The order to bow is qualified — *"bow down **with those who bow**"* — while no such qualification appears with the order to prostrate.

This, Maʿārif says, apparently seems to hint that **people generally do not observe due concern while making *rukūʿ*** (bowing). They tend to bend a little, then resume the standing position, as if in a hurry — a *rukūʿ* that is closer to standing (*qiyām*). So, Maʿārif continues, by mentioning the qualification *"those who bow"*, Allah Almighty has given **a model to be followed**, so that one's bowing in prayer could become similar to those who bow fully and perfectly, as is due.

**Living it:** the next time you go into *rukūʿ*, take it seriously — settle into it, let the back actually bow, do not treat it as the hurried gap between standing and prostrating. Maʿārif's reading of this one qualifying phrase quietly measures our *rukūʿ* against those who do it properly.

---

## Ayah 44: "You were not there"

Here the address shifts from Maryam to the Prophet ﷺ: **"This is a part of the news of the Ghayb (Unseen) which We reveal to you. You were not with them, when they cast lots with their pens as to which of them should be charged with the care of Maryam; nor were you with them when they disputed."**

Ibn Kathir explains the meaning: *"You were not present, O Muhammad, when this occurred, so you cannot narrate what happened to the people as an eyewitness. Rather, Allah disclosed these facts to you as if you were a witness"* — when they conducted a lottery to choose the custodian of Maryam, **seeking the reward of this good deed**.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** states what the ayah is doing argumentatively: this verse **presents an argument to prove the prophethood of Sayyidna Muhammad ﷺ**, by referring to happenings in the lives of Sayyidna Zakariyya (peace be upon him) and Sayyidah Maryam. These took place in the remote past, with no likelihood of their being seen or heard or read — especially by him ﷺ — which by itself proves that his being so informed of the unknown was **beyond the ordinary course of learning**. He had no way of finding out such details by any obvious means at his command. Hence, Maʿārif concludes, this information was revealed to him as part of the message he gave to others.

And Maʿārif notes how precisely the ayah puts it: he ﷺ was not there to see them drawing lots by throwing their reed pens in water — on a prior agreement that **the owner of the pen which flows against the current shall be the winner** — nor was he present on the scene earlier, when they were **quarrelling** about the custody of Maryam before agreeing upon the drawing of lots. The ayah names both scenes.

---

## The story behind the pens

Ibn Kathir preserves the scene. **Ibn Jarir** recorded that **ʿIkrimah** said:

Maryam's mother left with Maryam, carrying her in her infant cloth, and took her to the rabbis from the offspring of Aaron, the brother of Musa. They were responsible for taking care of **Bayt al-Maqdis** (the Masjid) at that time, just as there were those who took care of the Kaʿbah. Maryam's mother said to them: *"Take this child whom I vowed [to serve the Masjid]. I have set her free, since she is my daughter, for no menstruating woman should enter the Masjid, and I shall not take her back home."*

They said: *"She is the daughter of our Imam"* — for ʿImran used to lead them in prayer and took care of their sacrificial rituals. **Zakariyya** said: *"Give her to me, for her maternal aunt is my wife."* They said: *"Our hearts cannot bear that you take her, for she is the daughter of our Imam."* So they conducted a lottery **with the pens with which they wrote the Tawrah**, and Zakariyya won the lottery and took Maryam into his care.

**ʿIkrimah, As-Suddi, Qatadah, ar-Rabiʿ bin Anas** and several others said that the rabbis went into the **Jordan river** and conducted a lottery there, deciding to throw their pens into the river: the pen that remained afloat and idle would indicate that its owner would take care of Maryam. When they threw their pens in, the water took all the pens under **except Zakariyya's pen, which remained afloat in its place.**

Ibn Kathir adds that Zakariyya was also **their master, chief, scholar, Imam and Prophet** — may Allah's peace and blessings be on him and the rest of the Prophets.

Read this alongside ayah 44 and the character of the dispute becomes clear: they were not arguing over who would be burdened with an orphan girl. As Ibn Kathir puts it, they conducted the lottery *seeking the reward of this good deed* — and Allah settled it in a way no one could contest.

---

## A ruling that grows out of the story: drawing lots (*qurʿah*)

Because the ayah mentions lots, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses to state the ruling, citing *Bayan al-Qur'an*, according to **the Hanafi jurists**:

- **Not permitted:** *qurʿah* cannot be given a decisive role in determining rights **already known and fixed in Islamic Law**. Drawing lots in such a situation is included under **qimar (gambling)**. Two examples are given: something jointly owned by several persons, where a lot is drawn so that the one whose name comes out takes **the whole thing**; and a child whose parentage is disputed, where a lot is drawn and whoever's name comes out is taken to be the father. Drawing lots in such cases is not allowed in the Shariʿah.

- **Permitted:** as for rights which **depend upon opinion**, *qurʿah* is permissible in them — for instance, while allotting portions of a joint property, A is given the eastern portion and B the western by drawing a lot. This is permissible **because it was permissible even without drawing lots**, by mutual agreement of the parties concerned or by a decree of a judge.

Maʿārif sums the principle up: **where the rights of all parties are equal, and the purpose of the lot is only to allocate equal portions and decide which portion is for whom, then drawing a lot is permissible.** The lot assigns what is already fairly owed — it does not create or destroy a right.

---

## What the passage asks of us

- **Honour from Allah is a call to work, not a place to sit.** The moment Maryam is told she is chosen, she is told to be devout, prostrate, and bow. If Allah has given you something — knowledge, protection, a place near His house, a good name — ayah 43 tells you what to do with it.
- **Worship is preparation.** Ibn Kathir reads her increased worship as what readied her for what Allah had decreed. The devotion built now is what will carry what comes later.
- **Give *rukūʿ* its due**, in the manner of "those who bow" — Maʿārif's quiet correction of a very common hurry.
- **Compete for service, not for status.** The custodians of Bayt al-Maqdis disputed over who would get to raise a child, *seeking the reward of this good deed*, as Ibn Kathir puts it.
- **The Qur'an's account of the unseen is itself evidence.** Ayah 44 invites the listener to ask a simple question — *how could he ﷺ know this?* — and Maʿārif answers it: this was beyond the ordinary course of learning, so it was revealed to him as part of the message he gave to others.

passages.title: The annunciation and mission of Jesus
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is

These seven ayat are one continuous piece of news. The angels announce to Maryam that she will bear a son — and in the same breath Allah tells her, in advance, who that son will be and what he will do: his names, his honour, his voice, his education, his miracles, his mission, and the single sentence he came to say. Nothing here is a separate topic. The announcement runs straight through to ayah 51, where 'Īsā (peace be upon him) speaks in his own voice: **"Truly, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him (Alone). This is the straight path."** Everything before it — the honour, the wonders, the Scripture — arrives at that line.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the flow: the previous verse, ayah 44, stood parenthetically between these verses and ayat 42–43, and its purpose was to affirm the prophethood of Sayyidnā Muhammad ﷺ. With ayah 45 the account of Sayyidah Maryam resumes, and it is preparing the ground for a fuller account of the birth, mission and miracles of Sayyidnā 'Īsā (peace be upon him).

---

## The announcement and what is packed into it (45–46)

**"(Remember) when the angels said: 'O Maryam! Verily, Allah gives you the glad tidings of a Word from Him, his name will be Al-Masīh, 'Īsā, the son of Maryam, held in honour in this world and in the Hereafter, and he will be one of those who are near to Allah. He will speak to the people, in the cradle and in manhood, and he will be one of the righteous.'"**

Ibn Kathir says simply that this ayah contains the glad tidings the angels brought to Maryam that she would give birth to a mighty son who will have a great future. Notice how much is folded into so few words.

**"A Word from Him."** Ibn Kathir explains this as *a son who will come into existence with a word from Allah, "Be," and he was.* He adds that this is also the meaning of what was said earlier concerning Yahyā — *"Believing in the Word from Allah"* (3:39) — and this, he says, is the position of the majority of the scholars.

**"Al-Masīh."** Ibn Kathir gives the derivation: he was called Al-Masīh, the Messiah, because when he *touched* (in Arabic, *Mash*) those afflicted with an illness, they would be healed **by Allah's leave**. Even inside the name, the qualifier is already there.

**"'Īsā, the son of Maryam."** This, Ibn Kathir says, is the name by which he will be known in this life, especially by the believers — and the phrase relates 'Īsā to his mother *because he did not have a father*.

**"Held in honour in this world and in the Hereafter, and one of those near to Allah."** Ibn Kathir unpacks both halves. In this world: he will be a leader, honoured by Allah because of the Law that Allah will reveal to him, the Scripture sent down to him, and the other bounties Allah will grant him. In the Hereafter: he will intercede with Allah, **by His leave**, on behalf of some people — just as is the case, Ibn Kathir says, with his brethren the mighty Messengers of Allah, peace be upon them all.

**Speaking in the cradle.** Ibn Kathir explains what the infant speech was *for*: calling to the worship of Allah alone without partners, while still in the cradle, as a miracle from Allah — and when he is a man, by Allah's revelation to him. The content is the same at both ends of his life. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the scene: soon after his birth, when people chided Sayyidah Maryam on the basis of a false accusation, the newborn spoke up, saying *innī 'abdullāh* — "I am a servant of Allah." His first recorded sentence is a confession of servanthood.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites two narrations here, both from Abū Hurayrah. Muhammad bin Ishāq recorded that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"No infant spoke in the cradle except 'Īsā and the companion of Jurayj."* And Ibn Abī Hātim recorded that the Prophet ﷺ said: *"No infant spoke in the cradle except three: 'Īsā, the boy during the time of Jurayj, and another boy."*

**The puzzle of "kahl."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises a question worth sitting with. Speaking in infancy is plainly a sign and a miracle, and it belongs in a list of marvels. But speaking to people during one's middle age is very normal — something everyone does, Muslim or not, learned or unlettered. Why is it mentioned here as something special?

One answer, Maʿārif reports, appears in *Bayān al-Qur'ān* by Maulana Ashraf Thanavi (may Allah have mercy on him): the real purpose is to focus on the miraculous nature of *meaningful* infant speech. The reference to speech in middle age is there to indicate that his childhood speech too would not be the usual baby-talk, but rational, even learned and eloquent, as a man speaks in his advanced years. The discussion then continues in the same breath: looking into the true historical background of 'Īsā (peace be upon him), this reference to him speaking to people in his middle age provides a great standing argument in favour of the Islamic position — that, according to Qur'anic belief, he has been raised alive onto the heavens. Hadith narrations, Maʿārif says, prove that when he was raised he was in the approximate age bracket of thirty to thirty-five, youth at its best. Middle age — *kahl* in Arabic — was something he never reached during his life in this world. So his talking to people in his middle age can happen only when he graces this world once again with his presence. Just as his childhood speech was a miracle, his speech in middle age could be nothing else but another miracle.

**"And he will be one of the righteous."** Ibn Kathir: righteous *in his statements and actions*, for he will possess pure knowledge and righteous works. Knowledge and deed together — a pairing that returns at the very end of this passage.

---

## Maryam's question, and the answer that guards her (47)

**"She said: 'O my Lord! How shall I have a son when no man has touched me.' He said: 'So (it will be), for Allah creates what He wills. When He has decreed something, He says to it only: Be! — and it is.'"**

Ibn Kathir puts her thought into words: *"How can I have a son while I did not marry, nor intend to marry, nor am I an indecent woman, may Allah forbid?"* Her question is not doubt about Allah's power; it is bewilderment about how, spoken by a woman whose whole life has been chastity. Maʿārif frames the same question a second way: was this to be a divine miracle, or would she be asked to marry a man? The divine answer eliminates the second possibility.

**"Allah creates what He wills."** Ibn Kathir: He is Mighty in power, and nothing escapes His ability. Maʿārif adds that His will alone is all-sufficient to bring something into existence — He needs no medium and no cause; it is only His command "Be" which makes things come into existence.

Then a detail of wording that repays attention. Ibn Kathir observes that Allah used the word **"create"** here instead of the word **"does,"** as in the account of Zakariyyā (3:40) — and the reason he gives is exact: *to eradicate any evil thought concerning 'Īsā.* A single verb, chosen to keep a shadow from ever falling on Maryam.

**"Be — and it is."** Ibn Kathir: what Allah wills comes into existence instantly and without delay. He brings in another ayah, *"And Our commandment is but one as the twinkling of an eye"* (54:50) — meaning, as he explains it, that the command is issued once and the thing comes into existence as fast as, and faster than, a blink of the eye.

---

## The education Allah gives, and the signs He sends with him (48–49)

**"And He will teach him the Book and Al-Hikmah, and the Tawrāh and the Injīl."**

Ibn Kathir notes that the "Book" mentioned here appears to refer to **writing**, and that he has already explained *Al-Hikmah* — wisdom — in his commentary on Sūrat al-Baqarah. The Tawrāh is the Book Allah sent down to Mūsā, son of 'Imrān; the Injīl is what Allah sent down to 'Īsā, son of Maryam, peace be upon them — and 'Īsā **memorised both Books**. Maʿārif reads ayah 48 as recounting his august virtues: born blessed with the honour of learning from Allah — Scripture, wisdom, and especially the Tawrāh and the Injīl — and then sent as a Messenger of Allah to all the Children of Israel.

The teaching flows straight into the mission. Maʿārif observes that the message he carries will itself be his argument in favour of his prophethood, and that the four signs enumerated in ayah 49 were enough for those willing to believe.

**"I have come to you with a sign from your Lord, that I design for you out of clay, a figure like that of a bird, and breathe into it, and it becomes a bird by Allah's leave; and I heal the blind, and the leper, and I bring the dead to life by Allah's leave. And I inform you of what you eat, and what you store in your houses. Surely, therein is a sign for you, if you believe."**

Ibn Kathir works through them. The clay bird: he used to make the shape of a bird from clay and blow into it, and it became a bird **by Allah's leave** — a miracle Allah made for him to testify that He had sent him. *Akmah*: Ibn Kathir specifies **a person who was born blind**, which, he says, perfects this miracle and makes the challenge more daring. The leper: "a known disease." And raising the dead — again, **by Allah's leave**. Then the last: telling a man what he has just eaten and what he is keeping in his house for tomorrow. All of these, Ibn Kathir says, are a sign testifying to the truth of what he was sent with.

**Why these signs?** Ibn Kathir reports that many scholars stated that Allah sent every Prophet with a miracle suitable to his time. In Mūsā's time, magic was the trade of the day and magicians held a high position — so Allah sent him with a miracle that captured the eyes and bewildered every magician, and when they realised it came from the Almighty, Most Great, they embraced Islam and became pious believers. 'Īsā was sent during a time when medicine and knowledge in physics were advancing — so he brought the kinds of miracles that could not be performed except by one sent by Allah. Ibn Kathir puts the challenge as a question: how can any physician bring life to clay, cure blindness and leprosy, and bring back to life those entrapped in the grave? And Muhammad ﷺ was sent during the time of eloquent people and proficient poets — so he brought them a Book from Allah such that if mankind and the jinn tried to imitate ten chapters of it, or even one chapter, they would utterly fail, even in collective cooperation; because the Qur'an is the Word of Allah and is nothing like that of the creatures.

**A ruling noted in passing.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that making the shape of a bird was the making of a picture — something permitted in that Sharī'ah; in ours, its permissibility was abrogated.

---

## Confirming the old, and the one sentence he was sent to say (50–51)

**"(And I have come) confirming that which was before me of the Tawrāh, and to make lawful to you part of what was forbidden to you, and I have come to you with a proof from your Lord. So have Taqwā of Allah and obey me."**

Ibn Kathir: he came **affirming the Tawrāh and upholding it**. And the second half of the ayah indicates that 'Īsā abrogated some of the Laws of the Tawrāh and informed the Jews of the truth regarding some issues they used to dispute about — as another ayah says, *"And in order to make clear to you some of the points in which you differ"* (43:63). The proof from their Lord, Ibn Kathir explains, contained affirmation and evidence of the truth of what he was conveying.

Maʿārif spells out the same logic: the unlawfulness of some things in the earlier code would stand abrogated by the new one, and his station of prophethood was the conclusive argument for that claim of abrogation — with the signs from their Lord as the proof of his truth. *Taqwā* here — being on guard before Allah — is given its practical shape by Maʿārif: beware of any contravention of the divine commandments, fear Allah, and follow his teachings in matters of religion.

And then the last line, which the whole passage has been walking toward:

**"Truly, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him (Alone). This is the straight path."**

Ibn Kathir's comment is a single clause, and it settles everything before it: *for I and you are equal in our servitude, submission and humbleness to Him.* The one who healed the blind and raised the dead stands on the same ground as his listeners before Allah. And notice the order of his words: not "your Lord" alone, but **my** Lord first.

Maʿārif reads the ayah as the whole of religion in miniature: *"Allah is my Lord and your Lord"* is the ultimate in **belief**, and *"Worship Him"* is the ultimate in **deeds**. This, Maʿārif says, is the straight path — the path that perfects the ideal combination of beliefs and deeds, leads to the way of salvation, and is the source of communion with Allah.

---

## Living it

**Read the passage in the direction it moves.** Every honour named here is one 'Īsā (peace be upon him) *receives*: taught by Allah, honoured by Allah, sent by Allah, interceding **by Allah's leave**, healing **by Allah's leave**, raising the dead **by Allah's leave**. The passage lifts him as high as a human being goes — and then has him say, in his own voice, that Allah is his Lord as much as ours.

**Take Maryam's question as a model.** She asked *how*, not *whether*. There is a difference between a heart seeking to understand and a heart refusing to accept — and the answer she received, "Allah creates what He wills," is the answer to every impossibility a believer meets.

**Let "Be — and it is" reach your own affairs.** Ibn Kathir's gloss is that what Allah wills comes into existence instantly and without delay, faster than a blink. Nothing escapes His ability — not the child given to a mother with no husband, and not whatever you are carrying today.

**And the first words of that child.** Before any Scripture, before any miracle, the infant in the cradle said: *I am a servant of Allah.* That is the same claim ayah 51 ends with, and it is the one claim available to every one of us.

passages.title: The disciples' pledge and the plot against Jesus
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat capture the turning point in the mission of ʿĪsā (Jesus, peace be upon him): the moment he senses that his people have hardened against him, the moment a small band of sincere followers steps forward and declares its faith, and the moment his enemies move to destroy him — only to find that Allah's own move had already been made. What binds the passage together is a single contrast: the enemies' secret plotting on one side, and on the other a handful of believers who declare themselves helpers of Allah — and Allah Himself, who is "the Best of those who plot."

## The moment the mission changes

Māʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene. Following the blessed predictions mentioned earlier in the sūrah, ʿĪsā was born with all the promised signs. As a messenger sent to Banī Isrāʼīl, he presented his call to them supported by miracles that proved his prophethood. But they were adamant. They kept on rejecting him as a prophet, even going to the limit of being physically hostile to him.

Ayah 52 opens with the words *fa-lammā aḥassa ʿĪsā* — rendered by Ibn Kathir as "Then when ʿĪsā came to know" of their disbelief. Ibn Kathir explains the meaning: ʿĪsā *felt* that they were adamant in disbelief and continuing in misguidance. This is not the discovery that some people disagreed with him; it is the settled recognition that a door has closed.

Māʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out something easy to miss, and flags it under the heading "An Important Note." Ayah 52 states that ʿĪsā looked for helpers in the way of Allah **only when he sensed hostility from the disbelievers**, and not at the initial stage of his call. As is obvious, he had risen to the task all alone, obeying the command of his Lord, without worrying about setting up a "party" in advance. When the need came, he found a group around him. As Māʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, a little thought here would show that every worthy mission demands such determination and courage.

## "Who will be my helper in Allah's cause?"

The question in ayah 52 is *man anṣārī ilā Allāh*, which Ibn Kathir renders as "Who will be my helper in Allah's cause?"

The commentators read it in two ways. **Mujahid** commented: "Meaning, who would follow me to Allah?" — a call to join him on the road. **Ibn Kathir**, after reporting that, says that what appears more likely is that ʿĪsā was asking, "Who would help me convey the Message of Allah?" — a call for support in the work of conveying the message itself. The difference is whether the emphasis falls on following him or on carrying the message with him.

## The Prophet ﷺ asking the same question

Ibn Kathir places beside this ayah a scene from our own Prophet's ﷺ life, and it is the single most illuminating thing in his commentary on this passage. During the Hajj season, before the Hijrah, the Prophet ﷺ said:

> "Who will give me asylum so that I can convey the Speech of my Lord, for the Quraysh have prevented me from conveying the Speech of my Lord."

He kept asking until he found the Anṣār. They helped him and gave him refuge; he later migrated to them, and they comforted him and protected him from all his enemies — may Allah be pleased with them all.

(Ibn Kathir relates these words of the Prophet ﷺ without naming a ḥadīth collection, so the teaching stands as he reports it, without attribution to any named book.)

Ibn Kathir then says plainly: this is similar to what happened with ʿĪsā, for some of the Children of Israel believed in him, gave him their aid and support, and followed the light that was sent with him. The pattern is one pattern. A prophet is rejected by the many; he calls out for helpers; a few answer — and those few become the ones Allah names in His Book.

## Who were the ḥawāriyyūn?

Ibn Kathir gives the short answer: *ḥawārī* in Arabic means **support**.

Māʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word further. *Ḥawāriyy* (singular of *al-ḥawāriyyūn*, translated as "the disciples") derives from **ḥawar**, which lexically means **whiteness**. In religious terminology the title was given to the sincere disciples or companions of ʿĪsā for one of three reasons: because of their sincerity, because of the purity of their hearts, or because of their white dress. Māʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that, likewise, the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ have been called *ṣaḥābiyy* (plural *ṣaḥābah*).

Some commentators, Māʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, have given the number of the disciples as twelve. Incidentally, the word *ḥawāriyy* is also at times used in the absolute sense of "helper" or "supporter."

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir records from *the Two Ṣaḥīḥs* that when the Prophet ﷺ encouraged the people to fight during the battle of al-Aḥzāb, az-Zubayr came forward; and again, when the Prophet ﷺ asked for fighters a second time, az-Zubayr came forward. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> "Every Prophet has a ḥawārī, and az-Zubayr is my ḥawārī."

Māʿārif ul Qurʼān cites the same ḥadīth from *Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī*, glossing *ḥawārī* there as "a sincere companion." Note how the title was earned: the call for fighters went out, and the same man stepped forward both times.

## Their answer, and then their prayer

Their reply in ayah 52 is layered, and each layer matters.

**"We are the helpers of Allah."** The one they name in their answer is Allah.

**"We believe in Allah."** The support is built on belief.

**"And bear witness that we are Muslims."** They ask their prophet to be their witness — to testify on their behalf that they submitted.

Then ayah 53 turns the same content upward. Māʿārif ul Qurʼān makes this structure explicit: the text identifies the very first followers of ʿĪsā and brings to light their real creed, "expressed first before their prophet and then (in verse 53), reiterated it in the form of a prayer before their Lord." The same declaration is made twice, to two different addressees — and only the second one is a duʿāʼ:

> "Our Lord! We believe in what You have sent down, and we follow the Messenger; so write us down among those who bear witness."

Notice the two halves. *We believe in what You have sent down* — assent to the revelation. *And we follow the Messenger* — following the one who brought it. Faith and following, never separated.

Then the request: **"so write us down among those who bear witness"** (*fa-ktubnā maʿa ash-shāhidīn*). Having just asked ʿĪsā to bear witness *for* them, they ask Allah to write them down *among the witnesses*.

**Ibn ʿAbbās on this phrase.** Ibn Kathir reports that Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded that Ibn ʿAbbās said of "so write us down among those who bear witness": *"Meaning among the Ummah of Muḥammad."* Ibn Kathir adds that this "has a good chain of narration." Read that way, the first sincere followers of ʿĪsā prayed to be enrolled in the community of the Prophet ﷺ who had not yet come — a striking thing for a reader of this sūrah to sit with.

## Ayah 54: *makr*, and what the word really means

"And they plotted, and Allah planned too. And Allah is the Best of those who plot."

Māʿārif ul Qurʼān treats this ayah with unusual care over the language, and explains why the care is necessary. The Arabic word **makr** denotes *a subtle and secret move or plan*. If it is for a good purpose it is good; if it is for a bad purpose it is bad. That is exactly why the qualifier *sayyiʼ* (evil) was placed alongside *makr* in the verse *"And evil plan besets none but its perpetrator"* (35:43).

Māʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a caution that speaks directly to non-Arabic readers: in the everyday idiom of Urdu — the language in which the commentary was originally written — the word *makr* is used exclusively for conspiracy, evil plan and strategy, and therefore should not be equated with the Arabic usage. This, the commentary says, is the reason why Allah has been called here **Khayr al-Mākirīn**, "the Best of those who make moves."

So, on Māʿārif ul Qurʼān's reading, the parallel wording is not attributing the enemies' evil scheming to Allah. The ayah tells us that while the Jews were setting one thing in motion in secret, "the subtle and secret move made by Allah Almighty was countering their evil plans more effectively" — and Māʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that this counter-move is what the following verses go on to describe.

## The plot itself

Ibn Kathir tells the story. The Children of Israel tried to kill ʿĪsā by conspiring to defame him and crucify him. They complained about him to the king, who was a disbeliever, claiming that ʿĪsā was a man who misguided people, discouraged them from obeying the king, caused division, and separated between a man and his own son. They also said other lies about him — lies which, as Ibn Kathir says, they will carry on their necks — including accusing him of being an illegitimate son. Māʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the Jews' conspiracies went to the limit of convincing the ruler of the time that ʿĪsā was a heretic, bent upon changing the Torah and about to make apostates of everybody.

The king became furious and sent his men to capture ʿĪsā, to torture and crucify him. They surrounded his home, and he thought that they would surely capture him.

Then Allah saved him from them. Ibn Kathir relates that Allah raised him up from the house to heaven, and put the image of ʿĪsā on a man who was in the house. When the unjust people went into the house while it was still dark, they thought that he was ʿĪsā. They captured that man, humiliated him and crucified him, and placed thorns on his head. Māʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same account in brief: they sent one of them to arrest ʿĪsā, Allah changed that man's face totally and made him resemble ʿĪsā, ʿĪsā was raised to the heavens, and that person was crucified under the mistaken identity.

Ibn Kathir's conclusion is stark: Allah saved and raised His Prophet away from them, leaving them in disarray in the darkness of their transgression, thinking that they had successfully achieved their goal. Allah made their hearts hard and defiant of the truth, disgracing them with a disgrace that will remain with them until the Day of Resurrection. *And they plotted, and Allah planned too. And Allah is the Best of those who plot.*

Māʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that how Allah had planned to save ʿĪsā from their clutches was disclosed to him when his enemies came to arrest him, and that the details of those disclosures are mentioned in verse 55.

## Why the wording is explained so carefully

Māʿārif ul Qurʼān states its reason plainly. Some sects deny — "contrary to the belief of the entire Muslim community" — the ascension of ʿĪsā, his being alive in the heavens, and his descent in the later times, and they have worked through the words and meanings of these verses to open doors of distortion in the Qur'anic text. That is why, the commentary says, it seemed appropriate to explain these words in some detail.

## Living it

**Start alone if you must.** ʿĪsā did not build a following before beginning; he rose to the task alone in obedience to the command of his Lord, and when the need came he found a group around him. Māʿārif ul Qurʼān names this as the lesson of the ayah's timing: every worthy mission demands such determination and courage.

**Answer when the call goes out.** Az-Zubayr's title was earned by coming forward at al-Aḥzāb when the Prophet ﷺ called for fighters — and again when he called a second time. The ḥawāriyyūn came forward at a comparable moment: after ʿĪsā had sensed the hostility of his people.

**Say it to Allah, not only to people.** The disciples declared their faith before their prophet and then, in ayah 53, said the same thing again to their Lord as a prayer. A commitment announced publicly is worth little until it has been placed before Allah.

**Ask to be written down.** Their duʿāʼ in ayah 53 is a beautiful one to carry: *Rabbanā āmannā bimā anzalta wa-t-tabaʿnā ar-rasūla fa-ktubnā maʿa ash-shāhidīn* — "Our Lord! We believe in what You have sent down, and we follow the Messenger; so write us down among those who bear witness."

**And when the plotting closes in.** The last words of ayah 54 are meant to be a believer's rest. Whatever is being arranged in secret against the truth, Allah's own move is subtler still and counters it more effectively — and Allah is the Best of those who plot.
